title: Is Accumulated Depreciation an Asset on Your Balance Sheet?
summary: Accumulated depreciation is the cumulative total of depreciation recorded against an asset’s cost, and it’s recorded as a contra-asset on the balance sheet.
body_markdown:
When you’re updating your business’s bookkeeping, accumulated depreciation can be easy to misread. Is accumulated depreciation an asset or a liability? Do you enter the built-up loss of value of your equipment with other assets on your balance sheet, like real estate and cash, or with liabilities like debt and accounts payable?


These aren’t theoretical questions. Accumulated depreciation is a key element in planning for capital spending on new machinery, computers, and warehouses while also updating your financial records to reflect your business’s true profitability.


Here is what you need to know about accumulated depreciation, how to account for it on financial statements, and how it can affect budgeting, planning, and investment decisions.


## What is accumulated depreciation?


Accumulated depreciation is a running total of depreciation recorded against an asset since its purchase. It is recorded in the accumulated depreciation account as a contra-asset on the balance sheet.


[Depreciation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-depreciation) accounts for the wear and tear that erodes the value of fixed assets like machinery, computers, or vehicles over time. Businesses spread out depreciation of assets across accounting periods, typically over the course of years, based on the expected useful life of the assets. For example, if a company buys equipment for $10,000 with a useful life of five years, simple annual depreciation expense is one-fifth of the cost, or $2,000.


Accumulated depreciation increases over time as the asset value declines to a point where it is worthless or has only salvage value, meaning the price it might fetch if sold.


Assets such as factory machinery or trucks typically have some salvage value, also called residual value. For example, these types of assets might be sold as scrap metal. Other assets that depreciate quickly or become obsolete, such as desktop computer monitors and printers, may be worthless. In these cases, a business likely would assume no salvage value when establishing a depreciation schedule. It eventually writes the asset value down to zero and would face a disposal cost.


## Accounting treatment of depreciation


Depreciation is recorded as a non-cash expense on a business’s[income statement](https://www.shopify.com/blog/income-statement) . Accumulated depreciation, on the other hand, is recorded as a reduction in asset value on the balance sheet. Because they are non-cash accounting items, depreciation and accumulated depreciation don’t affect a business’s[cash flow](https://www.shopify.com/blog/cash-flow) , although they do affect taxable income.


Depreciation follows the matching principle of accounting, which allocates the cost of an asset to the periods that a business benefits from its use. If an asset is used for five years, for example, spreading its cost over those years gives a more accurate picture of annual profitability.[Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP)](https://www.shopify.com/blog/gaap) require businesses to depreciate assets this way rather than deducting the full cost in the year of purchase.


Understanding accumulated depreciation gives businesses a window into the productive value of their fixed assets and a timeline for when they might need to repair or replace those assets. New information technology, changes in consumer preferences, and expansion of industries and markets may require those businesses to buy new assets. Ecommerce companies can regularly review their accumulated depreciation to consider when to invest in new fixed assets.


## Is accumulated depreciation an asset or a liability?


Accumulated depreciation is neither an asset nor a liability. It’s not an asset because it won’t generate any future revenue, and it’s not a liability because it doesn’t represent an obligation or debt to repay. Instead, it’s classified as a contra asset, meaning it appears on the asset side of the balance sheet, as an offset to the asset’s original cost. The contra asset account appears just below the related asset; accumulated depreciation in the contra asset account is subtracted from the cost to show the asset’s net book value.


For example, let’s say a business buys production equipment for $10,000, and estimates the equipment will be used for five years. Assuming depreciation of $2,000 is taken equally in each year, the balance sheet entry after Year 2 might look like this:


ASSETS ****


Equipment, at cost $10,000


Accumulated depreciation -$4,000


Net book value $6,000


In other words, after two years, the equipment has declined in value to $6,000 from $10,000.


## How to calculate accumulated depreciation


- Straight-line depreciation
- Sum-of-years’-digits depreciation
- Declining balance depreciation
- Double-declining balance depreciation


Businesses have several methods for calculating depreciation, each spreading an asset’s cost across its useful life in a different way. The method chosen affects how much depreciation expense a business records each year and how quickly accumulated depreciation builds.


Two of the methods, straight-line depreciation and sum-of-years’-digits depreciation, include an upfront deduction from cost equal to the asset’s salvage value to determine depreciable value. Other methods such as declining balance and double-declining balance don’t assume a salvage value upfront, instead determining it at the end of the asset’s useful life.


Here are the key depreciation methods:


### Straight-line depreciation


The straight-line method is the simplest and most commonly used approach for calculating accumulated depreciation. It spreads the depreciable cost in equal annual amounts across each year of the asset’s useful life.


The straight-line formula is:


*(Asset cost − Salvage value) / Useful life in years = Annual depreciation*


As an example of how this works, let’s say a company buys production tools for $22,000. It estimates the tools will be used for five years and have a salvage value of $2,000. The depreciable amount is $20,000. Annual depreciation would be:


($22,000 - $2,000) / 5 = $4,000


With the straight-line method, accumulated depreciation grows uniformly by $4,000 through the asset’s life:


. Accumulated depreciation **Asset book value**


Year 1 **$4,000** $20,000 - $4,000 = **$16,000**


Year 2 **$8,000** $20,000 - $8,000 = **$12,000**


Year 3 $12,000 $20,000 - $12,000 = **$8,000**


Year 4 $16,000 $20,000 - $16,000 = **$4,000**


Year 5 $20,000


$20,000 - $20,000 = **0**


Salvage value $2,000


### Sum-of-years’-digits depreciation


The sum-of-years’-digits method is an accelerated approach that depreciates more in earlier years. Like the straight-line method, it deducts an estimated salvage value upfront and computes depreciation from the asset’s full depreciable cost during its life.


The formula for sum-of-years’-digits is:


*(Remaining useful life / Sum of the years’ digits) x Depreciable amount = Annual depreciation*


Still using the example above, an asset that cost $22,000 with a $2,000 salvage value has a depreciable value of $20,000, but the business assumes a shorter useful life of three years. The sum of the years’ digits is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Using this formula, the asset is fully depreciated in three years: 50% after the first year, 33.3% the second year, 16.7% the third year. This leaves a salvage value of $2,000.


### Declining balance depreciation


The declining balance method applies a fixed depreciation rate, expressed as 1 divided by its useful life, for the asset each year. This puts more depreciation expense in the early years and less in later years.


The formula for the declining balance is:


*Asset book value at beginning of year x (1 / Useful life) = Annual depreciation*


A business concerned about faster deterioration of assets, for example from wear and tear or obsolescence, might want to use this depreciation method. For example, the business above decides the production tools have only a three-year useful life. The depreciation rate then is 1 divided by 3 or 33.33%, and depreciation accumulates faster, starting at full cost with no salvage value deducted:


. Annual depreciation Accumulated depreciation **Asset book value**


Year 1 $22,000 × 33.33% = $7,333 $7,333 $22,000 - $7,333 = $14,667


Year 2 $14,667 × 33.33% = $4,888 $4,888 + $7,333 =$12,221 $14,667 - $4,888 = $9,778


Year 3 $9,778 × 33.33% = $3,259 $3,259 + $4,888 + $7,333 = $15,480 $9,778 - $3,259 = $6,519


### Double-declining balance


Double-declining balance accelerates depreciation by doubling the rate of the declining balance method. It’s more useful for businesses whose fixed assets lose most of their value in the first few years, such as computers and vehicles.


The double-declining formula is:


*Asset book value at beginning of year x (2 / Useful life) = Annual depreciation*


Sticking with the example above, depreciation would be double the rate of the declining balance method, or 66.67%. After only two years, the asset’s book value is almost fully depreciated to an amount close to salvage value.


## Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)


Any of the above methods can be used in accounting for net income and other financial statements. For federal taxable income purposes, the Internal Revenue Service generally requires businesses to use the[Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p946) for tangible property they begin using after 1986. Assets are assigned to a property class with a predetermined useful life, for example, five years for vehicles or seven years for office furniture. The IRS provides depreciation percentage tables based on the asset’s property class. An asset’s cost is multiplied by the relevant percentage to calculate depreciation, similar to a declining balance method.


Some businesses may be able to apply full depreciation in the first year. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in 2025, restored 100% bonus depreciation. It generally allows businesses to deduct the full eligible cost of qualifying assets acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025, in the year they are placed in service rather than depreciating that cost over several years.


MACRS depreciation is only used in preparing a business’s tax returns. It’s not compliant with GAAP, which requires use of the methods above to track the true economic value of a business’s assets, not its tax liability.


## Is accumulated depreciation an asset FAQ


### Is accumulated depreciation an asset or a liability?


It is neither an asset nor a liability. Accumulated depreciation is the total reduction to date of an asset’s value, which is subtracted from the asset’s original price to determine its book value, or its current accounting value.


### Where does accumulated depreciation go on the balance sheet?


Accumulated depreciation appears on the asset side of the balance sheet, under a business’s listed assets.


### What is the classification of accumulated depreciation?


Accumulated depreciation is classified as a contra-asset account on a business’s balance sheet, meaning it reduces the original value of the asset.
